items.question: What convinced you that robotics was approaching a breakthrough when Hugging Face began investing in it?
items.object: Robotics breakthroughs and the need for adaptable software
items.answer: I think honestly it started two years ago. We started our activities in robotics 18 months ago. At this time, there were a couple of breakthroughs out of these labs, where Stanford and these teams were starting to show robots that were able to tie knots, fold clothes, cook—throw things in the air on a pan and grab them. All of these things, in one way, used very little data, but also had a good perspective to leverage some of the world models and things like that that we see really benefit from internet-sized data. All of this kind of pointed to a short future where robotics were going to work in a way like hardware was already there, and in my opinion has been there for quite some time, but the missing brick was really software that could adapt, that could be dynamic, all of that. We started to see that, and that's why we started to work on the robot a little bit more than 18 months ago.

items.question: What is your vision for expanding robotics from a specialized field into a broad developer community?
items.object: Building a broad robotics community through accessible tools
items.answer: For us, the success of the robot—seeing this huge community—the big bet was: can you build a big community in robotics as well? There were small communities of hobbyists, or people very seriously building robots for factory lines, but it was kind of a tiny vertical in my opinion. The question was: could you move this tiny vertical to a full horizontal thing, just like nowadays every software developer is kind of an AI researcher almost? They all want to know how LLMs work, how you train them, and there's this very smooth transition where the 100, 200 million software developers are becoming kind of AI-aware. I think there is a potential future transition where all of these people also become roboticists in a way, if you give them the tools. That was kind of our goal. We started with the software library, and the success of that kind of brought us to also try to go into hardware, which is a big question as well. That's why we acquired our first hardware company this year, Poland Robotics, and we shipped—or at least, we opened the orders for—our first robots in mid-July. This went crazy.

items.question: How do you envision LeRobot reproducing the success of the Transformers library in robotics?
items.object: LeRobot
items.answer: LeRobot is our attempt of doing again the success of Transformers, reproducing the success of the Transformers library in the robotics field. This idea is having a central library that everyone would use and that would bring, in a very simple and accessible and easy way, all the latest technology, all the latest algorithms that people use to train robots efficiently, all the latest data sets that they use to train this, and also connect this to actuators, which is the hardware part of robotics. That's this intersection and this mix of three aspects: the policy, the models, the data sets, and the hardware, which we try to combine in LeRobot.

items.question: How do you see Hugging Face’s role in robotics compared with its role in language models?
items.object: Hugging Face’s role in robotics
items.answer: Our goal is to play the same role, which at a very, very high level is building communities and bringing people into this idea that AI can be open source, and it's not something you only consume, but something you can tweak, train, control, and host where you want. Actually, hosting where you want is even more important in robotics, because in a future where you have robots everywhere, you kind of want a lot of these models to run locally. If your robots lose connection to the Wi-Fi or something and then run into the wall, or maybe run into your kids, it's going to be much more dramatic than just an LLM hallucinating. Safety questions in robotics are a good reason you may want to be able to not depend on the distant API, but have the models as close as possible to the hardware. I would say our role is maybe even more important for safety and the future of robotics than it is in LLMs.

items.question: How do you judge whether the LeRobot community is on the right track?
items.object: Growth of the LeRobot community
items.answer: I should have checked the latest number, because it's exponentially growing. It's several thousand people. I would say six to ten thousand. A couple of months ago, we did a worldwide hackathon. We had 100 locations on over six continents. I would say it's still not in the millions of people, for sure, but it's way above several thousand people. The main indicator for us is we can measure the number of data sets on the Hub, for instance, and what we see in all of these things—the number of community members or data sets—we see this exponential growth, which is a very good indication that we're on the right track.

items.question: Why do you want to bring more polished, mass-market robotics hardware to the LeRobot community?
items.object: Mass-market robotics hardware
items.answer: You have to keep in mind that the hardware available right now is still very much hobbyist hardware. It's 3D-printed arms, with wires everywhere. That's why starting this summer we wanted to bring much more mass-market hardware: something that would interest not only hackers and people who are used to plugging cables everywhere, but also everyone in families, something that looks much more polished.

items.question: How do you understand traditional roboticists' interest in joining the LeRobot community?
items.object: Traditional roboticists joining the LeRobot community
items.answer: I would say one group is the traditional roboticists. They definitely want to use AI. A lot of them know how to build hardware and what they can use, but they've been frustrated by the limitations of the software stack, all the optimal control models, and how limiting all of these are for what you can do. These are people who have really happily joined the bandwagon. We see the same effect we saw in Transformers: many academic labs starting to use robots because it's a very nice entry point for all the students. This has been growing very strongly.

items.question: Why do you find the people entering robotics through LeRobot from an interest in AI especially interesting?
items.object: AI enthusiasts entering robotics through LeRobot
items.answer: The second community is much more interesting in my opinion. It's people who were not really into robotics, but because they're into AI and robotics looks like a physical manifestation of AI, they kind of want to go into robotics. These people cover software developers, but even people who are just interested in robotics. A good example is a lot of investors have actually bought S100's arm just to try to understand physically what this robotic thing is and what it can do. Because it seems so accessible, you get the arm, and the software is just Python code, and now with a little bit of vibe coding you can tweak it or control it quite easily. We see people who maybe are not purely technical, but want to understand what's happening in robotics, and they use this entry point, which is LeRobot. So you can vibe-code the robot.

items.question: Where do you see the most promising opening for an “iPhone moment” in consumer robotics?
items.object: The consumer robotics market’s potential iPhone moment
items.answer:
That's the thing I'm looking for, sometime called also the iPhone moment. What will be the first use case, the first moment where everyone, or a large fraction of the population, will think, “I want a robot,” in terms of consumer? I think the enterprise market is quite complex. In some places there's already a lot of robots in some industries, right? Car manufacturers are the best example. Then there's this second part, where there's an entry of robots, and here there are a lot of challenges around reliability: will these robots be reliable enough to be deployed in retail stores and be really useful?

The third part I'm much more interested in is entertainment, fun demos, education, where I think maybe the question around “I need a $3,000 robot because I need reliability” is less pressing. You can take a really accessible robot. Reachy Mini, for instance, is priced at $300. That's something that can definitely be an impulsive buy; you buy it as a gift, and you're not sure if it's going to work or not. But for this price, what we want to find is whether there's a lot of potential in entertainment, fun, education, learning AI through physical interaction, instead of just coding on a chatbot or on a screen.

items.question: How do you see Reachy Mini’s potential as a platform for consumer robotics?
items.object: Reachy Mini as an extensible platform for household robots
items.answer:
I think that's something that has not been explored at all. There were a couple of tries. The MIT Media Lab's Cynthia Breazeal did Jibo, for instance, but in the past they were usually priced a bit high, above a thousand, and more importantly, the software was very limited. You would buy a robot that would be fun, but you had maybe five or ten behaviors, and once you've tried them all, that's it. Here the goal for Reachy Mini is really to make kind of almost like a smartphone. It comes with a couple of behaviors, but because you can tweak it and people can build new behaviors and share them, and plug in new VLA, speech, and chat models, the possibilities are kind of endless. It's an open door on rebuilding the app store of the iPhone, basically.

That's what I'm very excited about. To be honest, this last part is still very much a bet, because nothing exists there; there's no real proof. What makes it quite plausible is this exponential growth of the community. You see Reachy Mini as the reincarnation of the robot dogs of the '90s, how people can play and experiment and have these robot companions in households.

items.question: How do you think shared data sets on the Hugging Face Hub could address the main data challenges in robotics?
items.object: Robotics training data and the Hugging Face Hub
items.answer:
I think the main challenge is in the data. There's just not enough data. There are some ways to use video on the internet as training data, but it's very limited. In some ways we may be able to use models, but in some others, if you want to automate a task, there's no way around just recording someone or the robot possibly doing the task.

I think here there's one possibility and one limitation. The main limitation is you can record a lot of tasks yourself, but usually what you'll lack is diversity. You'll be able to train a robot to do something very well in your room, when everything looks the same, but once you put it in the next-door room where maybe the walls are green instead of red, the robot has a lot of trouble generalizing. This is the main limitation. Our idea with the Hub was that everyone could record data sets, and if we managed to incentivize them to share the data, then we could maybe build a very multicolored, multilocation data set that would be extremely diverse and, hopefully, also very big. That's a long-term goal, and we hope this can help.

items.question: Why do you see robotics companies as receptive to sharing software and data openly?
items.object: Robotics companies' incentives to share software and data
items.answer: Another more direct thing we try to do is work directly with the actors of the community. We released a couple of data sets to try to help them release data sets. One of the nice aspects in robotics is a lot of people in the end want to sell the hardware, and so they can afford, even more than LLMs, to share a bit of the software as open source if it brings the whole field up, because that's not really directly what they sell. That's what I'm trying to convince a lot of robotics companies to do, and surprisingly it's something a lot of them seem interested in.

items.question: How do you explain the recent emergence of interactive world models?
items.object: The recent emergence of interactive world models
items.answer:
What's interesting is it feels like a couple of teams have been working on that independently for a few months, and they just happen to release this right now, right? When you talk about all of them, they are not really copying each other. I guess one thing was the advent of really cool, really good image generation, and basically finally understanding how to fix this six-finger thing and get a more reliable and coherent world model for images, which naturally was transposed to video. We see some really cool video models as well, and this is just one next step.

A lot of the founders I've talked to in this field also say they were helped by the advance of open source video model generation and open source image generation. They take this video generation model and fine-tune them, and then train them to be able to react to some inputs, which is also what we do in robotics. There's a lot of common points between these two things, and it seems to work quite well. You start to have this very interesting, totally new experience where you actually have a film that's controllable, photorealistic, and reacting in a coherent way to the action you input, which is either just moving around or asking it to add something, like a rider, castle, car driving. You see this thing that just reacts very well.

items.question: What potential do you see in applications of world models?
items.object: World models as tools for entertainment and simulated robotics data
items.answer: I think there's a lot of potential applications, both in entertainment—actually, some form of entertainment that might be totally new, something we've never seen, maybe the first time we create a new form of virtual entertainment—and in business. One downstream application is generating more data for robots. There are just two ways to generate data. One is to record it in the real world, which I think is still very interesting. The other is to simulate it. Surprisingly, on simulation we have not seen a lot of development; there haven't been real breakthroughs recently. Maybe this is the first breakthrough I've seen on simulated generated data in quite some time.

items.question: Why are you more excited about exploring alternative robot form factors than humanoids right now?
items.object: Humanoid robots versus alternative robot form factors
items.answer:
I'm quite more excited about trying other form factors right now. It's always quite expensive just because you need a lot of motors, and all the price in the robots is just the actuator. That's always like 70% of the price tag. When you have 60 actuators, that's just your bill. It's really hard to drive humanoids below the price of a car. I think the price of a car is already quite a high requirement. If you buy something at the price of a car, you do expect to have a lot of value out of it. That's why we're exploring smaller robots, like just one arm or just a moving head. There's some possibility that we can get cheaper humanoids at some point, and Unitree's been trying to cut the price. A lot of companies are trying, but it's going to be really hard to get this under $10,000.

The nice thing about the humanoid, of course, is once you've solved the humanoid, you solve a lot of tasks at the same time. If you solve the humanoid, you can do everything a human does, which is very exciting. The main question is, do you need to solve the humanoid? On my side, I would like to see a galaxy of different form factors.

items.question: How has seeing Unitree robots affected your view of whether the uncanny valley will limit social acceptance of humanoids?
items.object: The uncanny valley and social acceptance of humanoid robots
items.answer: I also think some of the other form factors are much cuter than the humanoid. For social adoption, I think the humanoid is also asking a lot from people. You're directly in this kind of uncanny valley where it's something that looks a lot like you, moves a lot like you. I thought this would be a big limit for social adoption. To be honest, I've seen a lot of Unitree robots; I don't know about you, but you kind of ignore them at some point. I'm also much more confident that people will just say, “Yeah, let's just...” Maybe we're too worried about the uncanny valley in robotics, and maybe at some point, once we've seen a couple of robots, people will accept them very easily.

items.question: How do you envision progressing from Reachy Mini and your small robots to a humanoid form factor?
items.object: Progression from Reachy Mini and small robots to humanoid robots
items.answer: The goal would be, if our Reachy Mini and our small robots work really well, that at some point we'll climb back to make it the humanoid form factor. I would say kind of progressively, as we've done bringing the community along with us.
quotes: The goal would be, if our Reachy Mini and our small robots work really well, that at some point we'll climb back to make it the humanoid form factor. I would say kind of progressively, as we've done bringing the community along with us.

rubrics.text: The response proposes bringing the robotics community along in the transition from small robots to a humanoid form factor.

items.question: Why would you prefer a future with many different robot form factors?
items.object: A future with diverse, accessible robot form factors
items.answer:
I would love to see that, because I think that's an option where we have many more robots in our life. What I would really not be super excited about is a future where robots are kind of an elite thing because they cost $100,000, and so basically if you're rich you have three robots at home, and if you're not, you don't. Hugging Face has always been about the big community, so we care about that. For this reason, I'm much more excited to see a lot of form factors that are accessible to a lot of people. Some are cheaper, some are more expensive, than just this single humanoid that costs a lot. If you can buy it, that's nice, and if you cannot, too bad for you. At Hugging Face, that's the future we try to nudge, to push toward.

I think it's also much more fun because in a way you're also restricting yourself, just like LLMs: if you just try to make them copy humans, it's one thing, but if you think maybe they can do something a human cannot do, it's also much more interesting.

items.question: How do you see the balance between large foundation models and smaller local models evolving as AI matures?
items.object: The coexistence of large foundation models and smaller local models
items.answer: I think we'll see more and more both. As the field evolves, we start to see really a long tail. For instance, if we take the downloads on Hugging Face, we see both very large state-of-the-art models being downloaded, which are usually too large to run on a local laptop. But some of the most downloaded models are actually just the right size to run quickly on a laptop. We see these two modalities, and as the field matures, we'll start to see this more and more. It's not like you choose one or the other. Depending on what you need, you might use one locally or not. GPT-5 with the router is a good example. Maybe the largest model, or the most reasoning, the longest reasoning chain, is not the answer to everything, and you actually need to smartly select the one you want. It can be behind a router, but it can also be just locally: you run some models here, and they might be extremely useful. We know better and better how to train models that are extremely useful, but when you need something much more complex, when you need reflection for a very long time, then you will turn to much larger models.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between open and closed AI models evolving?
items.object: The coexistence of open and closed AI models
items.answer: I think open source, just like in software, and both solutions, we just coexist. Having companies that open source both, or that do both—I mean Google has been an example for quite some time with the Gemma line and Gemini line, and some interesting moments where sometimes I heard that one Gemma model was actually so good it was better than closed source models, so they had to not open source it. The frontier is quite thin at the moment, in a way. The challenging new players are mostly in China, but I think we'll start to see some new foundation-model teams in the US. The frontier will stay quite thin, I think, and both things will be seen with a tiny difference in performance.

items.question: How do you expect the reasons companies adopt open-source AI to change as the market matures?
items.object: The reasons for adopting open-source AI as the market matures
items.answer:
The main reason right now, to be honest, at this exact point in time, is I think we're not exactly in a cost-saving time of AI. For a lot of actors, moving to open source because it saves cost is not the most important thing for them. Usually they move to open source because they want data privacy, they want to be able to adapt the model, or they have a new idea—like this action model, for instance. They have a new idea of something that does not exist and they want to do that. That's usually what we see right now: a lot of emulation of new exploration in an open source way.

What I do expect is, as we go to a more mature market, cost and being able to run it maybe on faster hardware or other types of hardware, and being able to own the model and the full stack where the models run, become more and more important. Just like in software, I think in the long term open source is a winning solution for many applications and use cases, but we're still in the turbulent place.

items.question: Why do you see resilience as an important advantage of open source AI for production applications?
items.object: Open source AI's resilience as a production foundation
items.answer: Surprisingly, I was doing these stats at the end of last year: this BERT model is still really used a lot. A surprisingly interesting aspect of open source is also resiliency. Once you have something that works in production, you may not want to be forced to move to the new GPT, right? That was a little bit of the backlash around GPT-5: people actually wanted to keep using GPT-4o for many things. Maybe they fell in love with it or it was their main friend, and some Reddit posts were around this, but maybe they just had their application, which worked really well, and they don't want to redesign it. I think the long-term interest for us is also to provide this very stable base: you build something, you know it will exist, and you know you can keep this as a very stable base.

items.question: How do you understand Hugging Face's evolving role in the open source AI ecosystem?
items.object: Hugging Face's evolving role in the AI community
items.answer: In general, I think in the community our role has switched progressively from pushing a lot of things ourselves, pushing our library, pushing our early product, to enabling more and more the community in general. We work now a lot with many actors of the community. We work a lot with llama.cpp, with VLM, with all the big players, to see how this whole ecosystem can be very efficient and work really well. When one model is released, you want to be able to use it directly in VLM, directly in LLaMA.cpp. We try to have more and more this role of meta-community builder, where we try to align and bring all the players at the same pace and help them move in the same way. In a way, we are much more focused on the community, on the Hub, than we were maybe a couple of years ago.

items.question: How do you understand China's emergence as a champion of open-source AI?
items.object: China's emergence as a champion of open-source AI
items.answer: Yeah, this is the most surprising thing that happened in the last two years: the fact that China would become a champion of open source. Who would have predicted that in the 2020s, right? I've actually been visiting them two weeks ago to try to understand a bit better on the ground how it's happening. The thing is, it's a very competitive market internally. There's a lot of teams there that are extremely good, and it reminded me in some way of Silicon Valley. People are working extremely hard, and all of these model providers compete with each other. One part on which they compete, which is surprising, is being the most open—the open source aspect. They're extremely proud of being very open. One of these companies that stopped being open, called Zhipu, decided not to open source it, and they saw an immediate backlash, mostly on hiring. People didn't want to come work there anymore, so they went back to open sourcing. I would expect this to continue, and I would expect quite more teams to come. We see that as well: when you have the presentation of GPT-5, a lot of people actually did the study. Some of them at Tsinghua University. We know the teams are here also, partly with Chinese members. They have extremely strong people, and they all really want to train the best model.

items.question: How do you assess the West's recent return to open-source AI?
items.object: The West's return to open-source AI
items.answer: What's interesting is to see the West coming back to open source very recently, just over the summer. This call for open sourcing: OpenAI decided to come back. Now we're just waiting for Anthropic to maybe open source their first model. I think it's time to try to ask them to participate. Right now the situation for open source is pretty good, but it's never like it's won. It's like the Jedi in Star Wars: we have to keep pushing this, keep pushing our flag of openness.

items.question: How do you understand the market incentives that lead AI companies to open source their models?
items.object: Market incentives for AI companies to open source their models
items.answer: I think one thing is when you have, in a way, nothing to lose, open source is always a good solution. It can be, for instance, you create a new company and you want to quickly rise to the top, then you open source your model. That's the Mistral recipe: how can you very quickly become a great player? For the Chinese, for instance, in the West almost nobody will use a Chinese API, so they don't sell APIs in the West anyway. In a way, they have nothing to lose from the Western market by open sourcing their model. I think there is this thing as players. The consequence is also that when nobody's open source, it's like a market: there's an interest for someone to take the room, to say, “We're going to be the open source player.” Meta was this open source player when everyone kind of stopped open sourcing. I feel like there will always be this thing: when some people stop open sourcing and there's a gap to being the only, the new top open source actor, then someone will want to fill this void.

items.question: How do you understand Western companies’ concerns about using Chinese open models hosted on US servers?
items.object: Western companies’ concerns about Chinese open models and model safety
items.answer: I don't see that a lot, to be honest. I try to do regular polls, ask a lot of people regularly what they think about that, because it can for sure be a concern. When DeepSeek came out, there was a very nice uncensored model from Perplexity, for instance. The thing is, in many business cases I don't think people really notice anything. I think there's more a general appetite for people to have a better way to understand the safety of a model. People are a little bit worried about having a model that maybe will behave strangely in some cases. This is a general thing a lot of companies have been asking: can you guarantee this model will always behave well? We know that's really hard because even with GPT, sometimes you ask the number of R's in “strawberry” and it's just behaving badly, and you're like, “Why? You're very smart; you should be able to know that.” This is a general thing that's needed soon, and there are a couple of teams working on that for sure.

items.question: Why do you see AI models for science as useful ground for thinking beyond human limitations?
items.object: AI models for science and human limitations
items.answer: Yeah, we build LLMs like humans. But what if an AI model could see infrared, could see some radiation we cannot? These are things humans cannot do. So it's already superhuman, and for science it's super interesting. A lot of the AI models for science are already superhuman in a way because they can either see a modality or predict things that are just inaccessible to humans. It's good, I think; it's good ground to think outside the human limitation of what we can do.

items.question: How have your experiences in physics and computer science shaped your understanding of access to scientific knowledge?
items.object: Access to scientific knowledge
items.answer:
For me it started a very long time ago. Before I was a lawyer, I was a researcher in physics. I was working on this superconductive material, and surprisingly, in superconductive material a lot of the great research had been done by the Soviets back in the Soviet Union. These people had a very different way of inventing theory than the Western world has, and they had some really great ideas and interesting things. But I had to find this invention or this theory, track them down in the Soviet GPT letters, and some of them were even still in Russian. From this time I got this idea that accessing knowledge is hard, and if I can make this easier, that's going to unlock a lot of really cool stuff. If I could just find where this equation comes from and really be able to read this article, that would be crazy.

When I joined computer science, I discovered arXiv, I discovered open source. I was like, this is really cool. Everything's just free, basically. Everyone shares things. It's written in English. Everyone can read it. It's even free; you don't even have to buy the publication. I was very excited about that until I started to try to reproduce one DeepMind paper, and I discovered there was a limit, because people publish what they want to publish but don't really give you all the tricks of the trade. When you try to reproduce that, you discover it just doesn't work.

items.question: What does open science for AI mean to you in Hugging Face's work?
items.object: Open science for AI at Hugging Face
items.answer:
Open science for me was this extension: it's nice to give open models to people so they can build things on top, but it's even better to explain how to train a model. It's a thing: it's nice to give a fish to someone to feed them, it's even better to teach them to fish. That's basically what we want to do. We think in the very long term AI is going to be such a fundamental technology that it should be just like physics, something everyone could learn by reading a book. If you want to learn today about general relativity, you can read a book and know about it. You don't have to pay to get access; you buy the book or find it, but that's basically free access. I think all the recipes to train an intelligent object or artifact should also be something everyone should know.

That's the very long-term thing, but the very short-term thing is if we teach people how to train great models, then they bring great models on the Hub and we have much greater content to offer. It's also just content providing. If we provide great models, it's nice. One example is we write very long blog posts; some of them even become books. We just published books this summer on how to train on a thousand GPUs, how to balance the load, and how to do all of this parallelism. Another very long blog post was about how to make a very good-quality data set. We made a data set to pre-train the models called FineWeb, and it's used in a lot of recent models. The Qwen models use FineWeb, for instance, in part. We also wrote how we built this data set, how we filtered it, and what's important to understand when you want to build great data to train models. All of these go together and are a way to bring better open source AI models in Hugging Face.

items.question: Why do you think treating AI-generated mathematical proofs as new science misses what makes a scientific breakthrough?
items.object: Scientific breakthroughs and AI-generated mathematical proofs
items.answer:
As always, it's nice there's some hype here because then it drives people, but I think sometimes we overestimate what's happening. Math is a good example. There was this idea: AI is doing new proofs for some math theorem, and that's like inventing new science. I think, as a scientist myself, that's really the wrong way to view science.

The reason is I was a bad scientist, so I can tell about that. I was a very good student. When you give me a problem, I'm pretty sure I can find the proof, I can find the thing. I know this thing has a solution, so I just have to fill the gap and grab a couple of things I know and combine them together. When I became a researcher, I discovered I was a pretty bad researcher, because what I was not able to do was ask the right question. If somebody asked me a question, “Can you demonstrate this theorem?” I could do it, but if someone said, “What is interesting to explore now in math?” I had no idea.

In science, the main thing you need to do if you want to do big breakthroughs is ask the right question. You need to find a way to ask a question nobody has asked before, a question that will open a whole new field of research. That's basically a Nobel Prize: someone who just opens a new field of research because this person asked the right question. Maybe the speed of light should be constant, and let's explore what that means; it means we can create general relativity, and then we can invent black holes out of it.

I know this thing has a solution, so I just have to fill the gap and grab a couple of things I know and combine them together. When I became a researcher, I discovered I was a pretty bad researcher, because what I was not able to do was ask the right question. If somebody asked me a question, “Can you demonstrate this theorem?” I could do it, but if someone said, “What is interesting to explore now in math?” I had no idea.

In science, the main thing you need to do if you want to do big breakthroughs is ask the right question. You need to find a way to ask a question nobody has asked before, a question that will open a whole new field of research. That's basically a Nobel Prize: someone who just opens a new field of research because this person asked the right question. Maybe the speed of light should be constant, and let's explore what that means; it means we can create general relativity, and then we can invent black holes out of it.

rubrics.text: The response distinguishes the ability to solve a supplied mathematical problem from the ability to identify a worthwhile research question.
The response identifies asking questions that open new fields of research as central to major scientific breakthroughs.

items.question: How do you assess the role of current large language models in scientific research?
items.object: Large language models as scientific research assistants
items.answer: I think LLMs right now are still extremely bad at this tasteful way to ask the right question. That doesn't mean we cannot do really cool stuff with them, but the way I see them nowadays is more as very useful helpers. Once human researchers say this is something interesting to study, you can use them to multiply by 10, 100, or 1,000 the prediction you can do. You can use them to quickly do a full survey of what has been done in the past on this molecule, this protein. You can use them to say, “What would be the most logical way to test this hypothesis?” But I still see this as an accelerator and assistant of scientific research. What I would love to see is an AI that would say, “Hey, I have an idea on how to go faster than light.” But for this, you cannot just write the answer on how to go faster than light; you have to ask the right question. What should we change to today's theory? What should we reconsider to invent something as groundbreaking as that?

items.question: Why do you see overcoming AI models’ tendency to agree with you as an important research question for science?
items.object: AI sycophancy and the development of scientific judgment
items.answer: I think it's related to something we talk a lot about: this sycophancy, the tendency of AI models to always agree with you. A good researcher is actually a good example of a person who disagrees. My former professor, who was a Nobel Prize winner, was very not friendly in how he would discuss, but I think that's part of it. You have to be extremely opinionated. Finding a way to push these models to have maybe stronger opinions, or maybe a taste in their opinion, I think for science will be key. It may, of course, be based on deep learning and LLMs, but it may involve other ways to train them, other ways to think about it. I think that's one of the big questions. Not a lot of people are exploring it; there are a couple.

The response suggests that developing stronger opinions in AI models could be important for their use in science.

items.question: What would you like people's relationship with AI to look like in ten years?
items.object: A future in which everyone can create with AI
items.answer:
What I would love to see is, in 10 years, a world where basically everyone feels like they can build with AI, and they're not just consuming AI, but they feel like they can be an actor in this thing. A little bit like the difference between we used to have a lot of media that were generated and created for us, and then we moved to the current era where everyone is actually able to create media. We saw that this creates a whole new generation of people, YouTubers and influencers, and people actually making extremely interesting content.

I would love AI to be the same: a very big community, like the software developer community, where everyone can create things with AI and they feel like it's just another tool in their box. They can code stuff, but they can also train a model and mess with, maybe adapt, the model. The nice thing about that is I'm a big believer in the creativity and natural invention of the community. I think it's something very beautiful to witness. In 10 years I hope people are not just consuming AI content and not doing anything, but actually exerting their creativity to build really nice things with a lot of AI tools around them. To be honest, that's kind of what we're building right now, so I'm quite optimistic. This thing is going to change a lot of things for society in general, because a lot of these jobs will just be different.
